title: Extraction and characterization of biocompatible hydroxyapatite (Hap) from red big eye fish bone Potential for biomedica

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states twice (abstract and methods) that '2 g of pulverized Priacanthus bone was treated with 2 M sodium hydroxide ... at 250 °C for 5 h' with no mention of an autoclave, sealed/pressurized reactor, or hydrothermal vessel. Aqueous NaOH solutions boil at ~100 °C at atmospheric pressure, so reaching 250 °C in a liquid-phase 'alkaline hydrolysis' step is physically impossible unless a pressurized/sealed system is used, which is never described. As written, the procedure is internally inconsistent with basic physical constraints.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results/Discussion section describing Figs. 2 and 3 (alkaline hydrolysis vs thermal calcination)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text first states 'Fig. 2 displays nanoparticles from alkaline hydrolysis of the HAp' and 'Alkaline hydrolysis of bovine bone... produces nanoparticles,' consistent with the abstract's claim of '50 to 80 nm' spherical particles from the novel alkaline method. It then directly contradicts this by stating 'Based on the results, alkaline hydrolysis HAps do not contain nanoparticles' and 'Alkaline hydrolysis produces HAp that is purer and has larger crystals than thermal calcination' — the opposite of the earlier claim that thermal calcination causes particle agglomeration into larger microstructures while alkaline hydrolysis preserves/produces nanostructure. The paper also concludes 'raw bone formed microstructure HAp when thermally calcined and nanostructured particles when alkaline hydrolysed,' which again conflicts with the 'do not contain nanoparticles' and 'larger crystals' statements made just sentences earlier.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion section preceding Fig. 1 description (citing ref. [27])
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The sentence 'CO₂, CaO, and (CO₃)₂ were kept at a high temperature of 1000 °C, whereas dioxygen, calcium oxide, and carbonate ions were eliminated from fishbone using the thermal calcination method [27]' is self-contradictory: it claims CaO and carbonate/CO2-related species are simultaneously 'kept' and 'eliminated' by the same thermal calcination process, and introduces the nonsensical term 'dioxygen' in place of oxygen/CO2 removal chemistry, making the described mechanism internally inconsistent.

The FTIR instrument is attributed to 'Bruker Tensor 27 Instruments, Billerica, MA, Germany.' Billerica, MA is a city in Massachusetts, USA (Bruker Corporation's actual headquarters), not Germany. Listing a US state abbreviation together with the country 'Germany' is a factually incorrect/self-contradictory attribution of the instrument's location.

The paper repeatedly describes FESEM (Field-Emission SEM) analysis and lists the instrument as 'SEM (JEOL JSM-5610LV Field Emission Gun).' The JEOL JSM-5610LV is a conventional tungsten-filament (low-vacuum) SEM, not a field-emission gun instrument, so labeling it as FESEM/FEG is inconsistent with the actual instrument's specifications.

The abstract concludes 'Cytotoxicity tests indicated no significant adverse effects, supporting the potential use of this HAp in biomedical applications' based solely on a single 24-hour MTT assay at two concentrations (12.5 and 25 µg/mL) with a reported 92% proliferation rate and no statistical analysis (p-values, replicate counts, or error bars) provided in the available text, which overstates the strength of evidence for biocompatibility and safety.
